Modular inventory management with Spring Boot

A modular inventory management system - products, suppliers, customers, invoices and stock movements in one Spring Boot application.

StockEase is the technical name of the repository and its codebase; the product ships to users as Bestandskontrolle, live at bestandskontrolle.vercel.app.

Java 21 · Spring Boot Spring Modulith PostgreSQL · Flyway Angular · TypeScript Angular Material ECharts Docker GitHub Actions Testcontainers · Vitest

Project overview

What it is

A bilingual inventory system for small businesses: products, suppliers, stock movements, invoices, reports. Java 21 and Spring Boot on the backend, Angular on the frontend, PostgreSQL. It runs in production at bestandskontrolle.vercel.app with a passwordless demo login.

Where it comes from

The business rules come from my working experience in manufacturing: no movement below zero stock, revenue only on paid invoices, low-stock alerts only for items ever stocked. Each rule is a decision I made and justified in 42 architecture decision records.

How it was built

Three roles, kept apart. A chat model designs and reviews: alternatives are weighed and specifications written there. An editor-integrated agent implements those specifications and reports what it did and where it deviated. Every domain and architecture decision is mine; I review every diff and merge every pull request. Where a specification turns out to be wrong about the code, the agent stops rather than forcing the change.

Why that is verifiable

Every change is a reviewed pull request. CI runs the full suite with coverage thresholds on both tiers; a regression cannot be merged. A new test is not trusted until it has failed for the right reason. Applied database migrations are immutable, comments included; a CI step enforces this after a comment edit once broke production startup. The history is public; each pull request states what was verified, what was measured, and what was left undone.

What you can see in two minutes

The demo (pick a role, no password). The decision log. The pull request record, especially #309 and #310.
